source.title: Analytic expressions for the output evolution of a deep neural network

record.tranche_reason: The study tests how training noise and batch size affect train and test error using analytic arguments and time-series regression experiments, rather than the image and language classification settings in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's discussion of prior work is not recorded as results. Numerical values in Figures 5–10 are not stated in the text, so the rows preserve the authors' qualitative descriptions rather than estimating values from plots.
record.test_reason: The study measures noise effects in time-series regression. Its batch-size experiments hold optimizer iterations fixed, so epochs vary with batch size; they do not test V5's fixed-epoch comparison. Explicit Gaussian-noise experiments do not compare batch sizes, and Hessian traces do not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that lazy-regime noise can prevent full training convergence without directly smoothing the output. Beyond the linear approximation, noise affects smoothness and suitably scaled noise can reduce the weight Hessian; their regression experiments show slight improvement with explicit noise and stronger improvement with batch size one. The Hessian interpretation is heuristic, and the higher-order analytical treatment uses scalar weights.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes noisy optimization and demonstrates effects in time-series regression; the versions concern other experiments and settings, including image classification, language modeling, and magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome changes between lazy and non-lazy training regimes, with training iterations and noise level affecting the reported effects; batch size also changes the SGD noise and outcome.

fits_no_version.finding: In lazy NTK training, explicit Gaussian noise increases training error without improving test performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explicit training noise need not improve held-out regression performance in the lazy regime.

fits_no_version.finding: After 10000 iterations with NTK scaling, explicit noise produces a slight test-performance improvement and greater variability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explicit noise can modestly improve regression performance after training departs from the lazy regime.

fits_no_version.finding: With regular scaling and 10000 SGD iterations, batch size one yields substantially lower test error on sine and temperature regression.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Smaller batches can improve held-out time-series regression performance under a fixed optimizer-step budget.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight-Hessian traces remain largely unchanged with noise in lazy training but decrease with more noise in the non-lazy experiments.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training noise affects weight-Hessian traces differently in lazy and non-lazy regimes.

record.problems: The numerical results are presented in figures without numerical values in the text. Experiments are on two time-series regression datasets, and the paper notes that classification may yield different results. The theoretical analysis uses a scalar-weight setting for higher-order expressions and treats weight-Hessian smoothness as a heuristic for generalization.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible results were left out.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under matched architectures and recipes.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error; approximation fidelity across widths is a different outcome.
Convolutional versus fully connected held-out performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects at fixed epoch budgets on image classification or language modeling, workload-dependent thresholds, and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects on held-out error across data sizes and regularization settings.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps among comparably fitted networks, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Remove both proposed V5 verdicts: neither the Gaussian-noise comparisons nor the fixed-iteration batch-size comparisons test that version. Figure 7 and Figure 8 also include temperature results, but these additional conditions do not supply evidence for any version.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not compare fitting natural labels with fitting random labels.
The study does not sweep width past the interpolation threshold.
The study does not compare convolutional and fully connected networks.
The study does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD.

The experiments use time-series regression and a fixed number of iterations, not image or language classification with a fixed epoch budget. The paper does not identify a workload-dependent batch-size threshold or test the recipe adaptations listed in the version.
The study does not test dropout.

The study measures weight-Hessian traces under changes to noise, but does not test magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness or compare its ability to rank generalization gaps against norm- or margin-based measures.
The study does not remove memorized training examples.

rows.size_stated: five layers, 200 nodes per layer unless otherwise mentioned
rows.operation_detail: Noisy training for 500 iterations, with Gaussian noise added in function space.
rows.value: A larger noise variance increases train error but does not improve out-of-sample performance.
rows.note: The text describes the plotted trend but gives no numerical values.
rows.check: Explicit function-space Gaussian noise is varied, not batch size. Unchanged test performance does not establish absence of V5's fixed-epoch batch-size effect.
